name: Sclera tattoo (eyeball tattooing)
lead: Scleral tattooing is the injection of pigment into the sclera, the white of the eye, to change its color permanently. Wikipedia reports no documented cosmetic use before the early 21st century; the modern practice is credited to body-modification enthusiast Shannon Larratt and practitioner Howie "Luna Cobra" Rollins around 2007.[1]

Published case reports describe serious complications including intraocular ink injection with endophthalmitis, retinal detachment and retinal necrosis, a sarcoid-type reaction, and unexpected lacrimal gland infiltration.[2][3][4] Ontario, Saskatchewan, Oklahoma and Indiana have restricted or banned the procedure, per Wikipedia.[1]
infobox: Banned in some jurisdictions (e.g., Ontario, Indiana)

paras: The procedure delivers dye between the layers of the eye, from where it spreads. Wikipedia says Larratt altered a photo around 2003 to give himself Fremen-style blue eyes and later worked with Rollins, with volunteers undergoing the procedure in 2007.[1] Larratt himself listed blindness among the risks and noted long-term effects had not been measured, according to the same article.[1]

A 2021 case report describes a man who received inadvertent intraocular tattoo ink injection and later developed endophthalmitis, retinal detachment and retinal necrosis, requiring surgery.[2] A delayed granulomatous uveitis after intraocular injection is also reported.[2] Other reports describe a scleral tattoo-induced sarcoid reaction[3], a French case report[4], pen-ink scleral tattoo complications[5], and a 2026 case of blue tears after infiltration of the lacrimal gland during tattooing.[6] Wikipedia also records media-covered cases with severe swelling and partial vision loss.[1]

Per Wikipedia, Oklahoma's Senate passed a bill in 2009 to ban the procedure, Ontario banned it in 2017, Indiana in 2018 and Saskatchewan in 2020.[1] The article notes the American Academy of Ophthalmology has published a clinical video on a case gone wrong.[1]
No systematic studies or trials were found. The evidence consists of published case reports describing complications.[2][3][4][5][6]

timeline.event: First reported volunteers receive modern scleral tattoos (Larratt and Rollins).[1]
Oklahoma Senate passes bill to ban the procedure.[1]

card.summary: Injecting ink into the white of the eye to change its color; permanent, with case reports of serious vision-threatening complications.
card.note: Case reports of uveitis, retinal detachment and vision loss; banned in some jurisdictions.

quick.overview:
Scleral tattooing injects pigment into the white of the eye to permanently color it. It emerged from body-modification culture in the mid-2000s.

It is a cosmetic modification rather than a treatment, and published literature consists of case reports of complications.
quick.mechanism: Ink is injected under the conjunctiva or into the sclera layers, where it spreads and stays.
quick.risks: Case reports describe uveitis, endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, vision loss and other reactions. Ontario, Saskatchewan, Indiana and Oklahoma have restricted or banned it, according to Wikipedia.
